Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

acute dystonia · akathisia · parkinsonism · tardive dyskinesia · neuroleptic malignant syndrome · metabolic and prolactin effectsWhich effect, timed from the start or the last dose increase, and what is the next step?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Time the effect from the start or the last dose increase:

  • Acute dystonia: hours to days; also after antiemetics such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine; give an anticholinergic
  • Akathisia: within weeks; lower the dose, switch, or add propranolol
  • Parkinsonism: within weeks; lower the dose; amantadine or an anticholinergic
  • Tardive dyskinesia: months to years; stop anticholinergics; a VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor if moderate to severe
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: days to weeks, evolving over 1 to 3 days, including with second-generation drugs; stop the drug, cool, give fluids

Serotonin syndrome comes within hours of a serotonergic change, such as an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor), with clonus and hyperreflexia; neuroleptic malignant syndrome comes over days to weeks with rigidity.

Clozapine and olanzapine carry the greatest metabolic risk; screen at least yearly.

Diagnosis
Which effect Acute dystonia – sustained spasm of the neck, jaw, eyes or tongue · Akathisia – internal restlessness and a compelling urge to move · Parkinsonism – tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, masked face, shuffling gait; reversible · Tardive dyskinesia – repetitive lip smacking, tongue and jaw movements, cheek puffing · Neuroleptic malignant syndrome – mental status change, fever, rigidity, autonomic instability; the creatine kinase (CK) can be very high
Management and treatment
Next step by effect
EffectFirst stepThen or also
Acute dystoniaA parenteral anticholinergic: benztropine or diphenhydramine; relief usually within 10 to 30 minutesLaryngeal spasm: assess the airway; intravenous anticholinergic
AkathisiaLower or stop the dose, or switch (eg, quetiapine, olanzapine)Propranolol
ParkinsonismLower or stop the doseAmantadine or an anticholinergic
Tardive dyskinesiaStop anticholinergics; they may worsen itModerate to severe: valbenazine or deutetrabenazine
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeStop the antipsychotic; aggressive cooling; correct volume and electrolytesBromocriptine or dantrolene are options
By drug Metabolic – greatest with clozapine and olanzapine; lowest with aripiprazole, risperidone, ziprasidone and high-potency first-generation drugs; at least yearly screening · Prolactin – any first-generation drug or risperidone: galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction, bone loss · Clozapine – severe neutropenia, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, seizures, profound hypotension; check the ANC (absolute neutrophil count) before and during treatment
Practice
  1. 23-year-old man given intramuscular haloperidol for agitation 8 hours ago now his neck is twisted to the right and his eyes are fixed upward Alert; speaks clearly; no stridor T 37.1 °C · HR 104/min · BP 138/84 mm Hg → Benztropine → acute dystonia within hours of a dopamine blocker: an anticholinergic such as benztropine gives rapid relief; dantrolene belongs to neuroleptic malignant syndrome and propranolol to akathisia
  2. 19-year-old woman in the emergency department for vomiting 1 hour after intravenous metoclopramide: jaw clenched, tongue pushing out, words slurred Fully alert; no lip or tongue swelling; no wheeze BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 96/min → Diphenhydramine → an antiemetic dopamine blocker caused acute dystonia: a parenteral anticholinergic such as diphenhydramine usually works within 30 minutes; dantrolene belongs to neuroleptic malignant syndrome and propranolol to akathisia
  3. 34-year-old man started haloperidol 2 weeks ago for schizophrenia cannot sit through visits; paces, shifts his legs, says he feels driven to move voices quieter; dose cannot be lowered HR 82/min · no rigidity or tremor → Add propranolol → inner restlessness with a compelling urge to move within 4 weeks of starting is akathisia; propranolol treats it when the dose cannot be lowered; more haloperidol would worsen it, and valbenazine is for tardive dyskinesia
  4. 46-year-old woman whose risperidone dose was doubled 3 weeks ago both hands shake at rest; slower walking with short steps; blank face No lip smacking or tongue movements T 36.9 °C · cogwheel rigidity both arms · alert, oriented → Drug-induced parkinsonism → tremor, rigidity, slow shuffling gait and masked face within weeks of a dose increase; tardive dyskinesia comes months to years later with orofacial movements, and there is no fever or altered mental status
  5. 58-year-old man with schizophrenia on haloperidol for 9 years constant lip smacking and tongue darting that embarrass him and disrupt eating takes benztropine as well BP 128/80 mm Hg · no tremor or rigidity → Stop benztropine and start valbenazine → orofacial movements after years of a dopamine blocker are tardive dyskinesia; anticholinergics may worsen it and should be stopped, and moderate to severe disease is treated with a VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor
  6. 52-year-old man started on risperidone for schizophrenia 6 days ago now disoriented, diaphoretic and rigid in all limbs T 40.3 °C · BP 172/100 mm Hg · HR 118/min · reflexes normal, no clonus · creatine kinase 24,000 U/L → Neuroleptic malignant syndrome → fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability and a high CK developing over days, even from a second-generation drug; serotonin syndrome comes within hours with clonus and hyperreflexia; acute dystonia is a localized spasm of the neck, jaw, eyes or tongue
  7. 29-year-old woman started on haloperidol in hospital 4 days ago rigid, confused, febrile; creatine kinase rising No new serotonergic drugs T 39.8 °C · HR 120/min · BP 164/98 mm Hg · urine dark → Stop haloperidol; cool; give fluids → neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stopping the drug is paramount, then aggressive cooling and fluids; another antipsychotic can cause it too, an anticholinergic does not treat it, and bromocriptine or dantrolene are options beyond supportive care
  8. 32-year-old man with schizophrenia stable on olanzapine for 1 year gained 14 kg; new fasting glucose 128 mg/dL Wants to stay on an antipsychotic BMI (body mass index) 33 kg/m² · BP 136/86 mm Hg · triglycerides 260 mg/dL → Aripiprazole → metabolic disturbances are greatest with clozapine and olanzapine, intermediate with quetiapine and lowest with aripiprazole; screen at least yearly
  9. 27-year-old woman with schizophrenia on risperidone for 8 months no periods for 4 months; milky nipple discharge Urine pregnancy test negative; no headaches TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) normal · BP 110/70 mm Hg · visual fields full → Dopamine blockade raising prolactin → risperidone, like any first-generation drug, commonly raises prolactin, causing amenorrhea and galactorrhea; a normal TSH argues against hypothyroidism, and risperidone commonly raises prolactin, so the drug is the likely cause
Pairs with SSRI Adverse Effects: hours after a serotonergic change, with clonus? Schizophrenia: Long-Term Care: monitoring the maintenance drug, with yearly metabolic screening?
Transferable rule

Time the movement from the start or the last dose increase before naming it: hours to days is dystonia, weeks is akathisia or parkinsonism, months to years is tardive dyskinesia.
